one_line: DigitalOcean's Archana Kamath and Tyler Gillam argue for per-request model routing chosen by task, cost, latency and rules, validated with your own evals. A live OpenCode demo shows roughly 3x lower session cost at similar quality, though the evidence is one vendor demo.
summary: The talk argues that teams should stop picking one model from a public benchmark and instead route each request to a model that fits the task, cost budget, latency need and user preference. Three pressures are named: spend (cost), fit (overkill of frontier models for simple tasks) and risk (no failover when one model degrades). Tyler Gillam then shows DigitalOcean's inference router, which uses a small open routing model (under 200 ms per decision, per the speaker) that reads natural-language task descriptions plus cost/latency/quality settings and optional decision-tree rules. A per-task config is shown with two selection styles: a manual ranked list with failover, and a "fastest in the last ~30 minutes" policy. In a side-by-side OpenCode demo, the router session cost $0.08 vs $0.25 after one feature task and $0.14 vs $0.44 after three tasks, with output quality judged as similar. A router-vs-Opus eval scored 90% vs 95% on correctness, which the speaker called within LLM-as-judge margin of error. The speakers frame routing as a base layer for evals, caching and personalization. Evidence is a single live run, a judge-scored eval with no methodology shown, and a vendor pitch, so the numbers are directional only.

key_ideas.idea: There is no single best model; the right model depends on the request
key_ideas.detail: Fit depends on the task, the system prompts and tools around the model, the cost you will accept, the latency the use case needs, and end-user preference. Public leaderboards cannot encode these. Examples: small open models for classification, faster larger models for inline completion, mid open-weight for code gen and bug fixing, frontier for code review and security.

key_ideas.idea: Three reasons to break the one-model habit: cost, fit and risk
key_ideas.detail: Cost: companies are capping usage (speaker names Walmart, Uber, Microsoft without data). Fit: frontier rates for simple work is overkill. Risk: a single model has no failover when it goes down or degrades. The speaker calls model orchestration the new FinOps.

key_ideas.idea: Auto-routing was a black box; make the routing rules editable and evaluable
key_ideas.detail: Earlier auto-routers chose a model with no way to fix bad choices. The described design takes a request through an open proxy (Plano) and a routing model. The user states costs, latency, quality, preferred models and hard rules in natural language; decision-tree rules can be layered on presets.

key_ideas.idea: Use the loop: route, evaluate on your own tests, adjust, feed results back
key_ideas.detail: The speakers stress that the router must be validated with your own evaluations, not a public leaderboard. The demo's eval compared router vs Opus on the same tasks, scoring correctness (90% vs 95%) and token use and speed, and the speaker said the gap was within LLM-as-judge noise.

key_ideas.idea: Per-task pools with explicit selection policies and failover
key_ideas.detail: Each task (bug fixing, code generation, test writing) gets its own model pool. One task uses manual ranking, so a preferred model is always tried first with a named fallback. Another uses a fastest-recently policy (about a 30-minute window). The same prompt can map to different models on different tasks.

key_ideas.idea: Savings show up across a whole agent session, not one prompt
key_ideas.detail: The live OpenCode comparison ran the same prompts through a single-model session (Opus) and a routed session. Cost was tracked across steps: $0.08 vs $0.25 after a feature task, and $0.14 vs $0.44 after tests and a README, with similar output quality by the presenters' own vibe check.

techniques.name: Per-task model pools with ordered failover
techniques.how: Define named tasks (bug fixing, code gen, test writing). For each, list candidate models and use manual ranking so the preferred model is tried first and the next one is a fallback on failure. Optionally pick the model with the best recent latency over a short window (about 30 minutes in the demo).
techniques.when: When you want a predictable primary model with graceful degradation, or when latency varies by provider and you want the fastest recent option.

techniques.name: Natural-language routing preferences plus hard rules
techniques.how: Describe each task in plain language and set cost, latency and quality priorities. Start from a preset, then add decision-tree rules for hard constraints. A small dedicated routing model maps each request to a candidate, so the choice is per request.
techniques.when: When you cannot hand-write a classifier for every request type, but still need explicit constraints such as never sending security review to a small model.

techniques.name: Side-by-side routed vs single-model agent runs with live cost tracking
techniques.how: Run the same prompt sequence through two agent sessions in the same coding CLI: one pinned to a frontier model, one routed. Show per-step model choice, token use, latency and cumulative session cost, then compare outputs.
techniques.when: When you want quick evidence that routing cuts cost on real agent workflows before running a formal eval.

techniques.name: Eval-gated routing with feedback loop
techniques.how: Score the routed system against a frontier baseline on your own task set using LLM-as-judge plus token and latency metrics. Adjust task descriptions or pools based on failures, then re-run.
techniques.when: Before trusting a router in production, and after any change to models or task definitions. Treat differences inside judge noise as ties.

numbers.claim: Routing decision latency under 200 ms per request (speaker claim)
Routing service described as free to customers; speaker says the routing model beat GPT-5-series models at routing with a fraction of the latency (vendor claim, no data shown)
Router vs Opus eval on the demo's task set: correctness 90% vs 95%, described as within LLM-as-judge margin of error; router used noticeably fewer tokens and was faster
OpenCode demo, feature request: session cost $0.08 (router) vs $0.25 (Opus), about 3x
OpenCode demo, after tests and README: session cost $0.14 (router) vs $0.44 (Opus)
Routing decision under 200 ms, custom mixture-of-experts routing model, zero application code changes needed (speaker)
Companies capping AI spend: Walmart, Uber, Microsoft (named by speaker, no figures given)

hot_takes: Model orchestration is the new FinOps, and it will mature in months, not the 15 years cloud cost optimization took.
Benchmarks only tell part of the story; your own task preferences tell the rest.
Routing is the foundation layer, not the destination; evals, caching and personalization should sit on top of it.

relevance.why: L1 Govrix Scout already has strategy routing. The talk gives a concrete design: per-task pools, ordered failover, recent-latency selection, and cost/quality comparison against a frontier baseline.
relevance.action: Compare Scout's strategy routing against per-task pools with ordered failover and a recent-latency policy, and add an eval that scores routed vs frontier-pinned output on cost, tokens and judged correctness.

relevance.why: ProsHarness drives Claude Code. Per-step model choice could cut cost on simple steps, but the talk does not address harness checkpointing or plan/critique flows.
relevance.action: Log per-step model and cost in a ProsHarness run and check whether simple steps (for example test writing) can move to a cheaper model without quality loss.

relevance.why: Matches the recurring interest in cheap-model (Haiku) pipelines. The talk's claim is that small models suit classification and labeling, and its method is judge-scored eval against a frontier baseline.
relevance.action: Run a small-model vs frontier judged eval on one classification or labeling step from an existing pipeline, and record cost and accuracy.
